_meta: A series of scrapes of a cumulative request counter, one of which follows a process restart, used to show that computing a rate as the plain difference between consecutive readings goes negative and undercounts when the counter resets, while a reset-aware difference stays non-negative and recovers the true increase. A cumulative counter (requests_total, bytes_sent, errors_total) only ever increases while a process runs, and a monitoring system samples it every scrape interval and reports the per-interval increase as current minus previous. That is correct until the process restarts: the counter is re-created at zero, so the reading drops from a large value to a small one, and current minus previous is a large NEGATIVE number -- an impossible 'rate' for a counter that can only go up. On a dashboard it shows as a sharp downward spike or a nonsensical negative throughput, and any total built by summing the deltas is short by roughly the pre-restart value, because the negative delta subtracts real traffic that happened. The fix is to notice the reset: when a reading is smaller than the one before it, the counter restarted, so the increase since the last scrape is the new reading itself (the rise from zero), not new minus old. This is exactly what a monitoring system's rate() and increase() functions do. On this fixture the counter climbs, restarts once, and climbs again; the plain difference produces a negative delta and a low total, while the reset-aware difference is non-negative throughout and its total matches the real in-window increase. The scrape readings are the fixture; every plain and reset-aware delta, both totals, and the reset detection are computed. Stdlib only.
